173.subtitle: Mother of everything, and free of every colour

commentary.meaning: Eight names that keep changing the distance from which she is seen. The verse opens at the largest possible scale — mother of all that exists, and then upholder of the moving world, the two words for the world chosen so that the first means the totality and the second what lives and goes about in it. Immediately after this the poem comes close enough to look at her face: wide-eyed, in the idiom that Sanskrit poetry reserves for beauty. And immediately after that it takes the colour out of the picture, calling her virāgiṇī, without passion, on a word whose literal sense is undyed. The second line describes a temperament rather than a cosmology. She is bold, assured, past hesitation; her generosity has no ceiling; her gladness is of the highest order, on a word that also names a fragrance which spreads by itself; and the last name says that she is made of mind, so that the faculty in which the whole verse has been forming its pictures turns out to be her too.
commentary.history:
The two words for world in the first line are not interchangeable and the hymn is using both deliberately. Viśva is the older and flatter of them: all, entire, the whole of a thing, and by extension the universe considered as a total. Jagat is a participle. It comes from √gam, to go, in a reduplicated form, and its literal sense is the going, the moving — the world named by the fact that it does not stand still, and by ordinary extension the world of living beings as opposed to the fixed and inanimate. So viśvamātā claims maternity of everything whatever, and jagaddhātrī claims custody of what moves. Dhātrī, from √dhā, to place, set, hold, has the same double reach: it is the cosmic term for what upholds, and it is also the everyday word for a wet-nurse. The compound thus says at once that she keeps the world in existence and that she feeds it.

Jagaddhātrī later became a goddess in her own right rather than an epithet. In Bengal she has an established autumn festival of her own, celebrated with particular grandeur at Chandannagar and Krishnanagar, with an iconography — lion mount, four arms — distinct from Durgā's. Nothing in this hymn refers to that cult, which is later and regional, but a reader who has met the name in that context should know that its appearance here is the older, general use.

Viśālākṣī is likewise both epithet and proper name. Long, wide eyes are the standard mark of beauty in Sanskrit description, where the eye is conventionally said to reach nearly to the ear and is compared to a lotus petal or a fish; the epithet is applied to human heroines constantly. It is also the name under which the goddess is worshipped at Vārāṇasī, in a temple counted among the seats where a part of Satī's body is said to have fallen. Whether the hymn intends the temple or the description, the effect within the verse is a sudden shift of scale: two names of cosmic maternity, then a face.

Virāgiṇī repays slowing down, because the English word dispassion loses what the Sanskrit is doing. Rāga is a noun from √rañj, to be dyed or coloured. Its first sense is colouring; passion is the derived sense, on the metaphor of a mind taking a dye from its object. The same word names a mode in music, a mood that colours the hearer. Vi- negates, so virāga is the state of being uncoloured, and virāgiṇī, with the possessive suffix, is she who has that state. Placed directly after a name about the appearance of her eyes and directly before a run of names about delight and generosity, it prevents both readings from going too far. She is looked at and is not thereby something that takes a tint from being looked at.

The second line is drawn from the vocabulary of persons rather than principles. Pragalbhā means confident, mature, capable of speaking up; in the classification of heroines used by the Sanskrit dramatists and rhetoricians it is a technical term, naming the woman who is past the hesitancy of the mugdhā and knows exactly what she is doing. The hymn has used this register before, in vidagdhā some verses earlier, and the two names belong to the same world of courtly aesthetic judgement. Paramodārā and parāmodā are then a deliberate pair, differing only in where the long vowel falls: parama plus udāra, supremely generous, and para plus āmoda, of the highest gladness. Udāra means noble and exalted before it means open-handed; āmoda means gladness and also diffusive fragrance, the scent that fills a room without being carried, and the second sense is why the tradition likes the name — her joy propagates on its own.

Manomayī closes the verse with a term straight out of the Upaniṣads. The Taittirīya's second section builds the well-known series of sheaths, each inner one described as the self of the one outside it, and the manomaya, made of mind, is the third of them. The suffix -maya means consisting of, made out of, as in hiraṇmaya, made of gold. The commentators generally read the name in two directions at once: she is what the mental sheath is made of, and she is the mind of every being who has one. Taken with the first name of the verse, the effect is a closed circuit — the mother of everything is the substance of the thought that is at this moment considering her.
commentary.practice:
Both halves of the first line are four and four; the second line runs three and five, then four and four. Pragalbhā is the only short name in the verse and it wants to be hurried. Give its three syllables their weight and the second line will keep its shape.

The most instructive sound in the verse is the join in jagaddhātrī. The elements are jagat and dhātrī, and a final t before a voiced aspirate becomes voiced: t plus dh gives ddh. What is written and said is a doubled dental with the aspiration on the second half — hold the tongue at the teeth for a full beat, then release with breath into the ā. Reciters commonly produce a single d with an h after it, which loses the length the metre needs.

Viśālākṣī contains kṣ, the cluster that gives learners the most trouble in the whole language. It is a velar k followed immediately by the retroflex sibilant ṣ, the tongue moving from the soft palate to the curled-back position without a vowel between. It is not the English x of "axe", and it is not the sh of "shy". The two ś sounds of the verse — in viśvamātā and viśālākṣī — are the palatal sibilant, made with the blade of the tongue against the hard palate, and are distinct from that retroflex ṣ; the verse gives you both within four syllables of each other, which makes it a useful drill.

Paramodārā and parāmodā are the trap. Both are five and four syllables of the same three sounds in nearly the same order, and both hide a vowel-sandhi: parama plus udāra gives o where the a and u meet, para plus āmoda gives a long ā where a meets ā. Say them slowly as pa-ra-mo-dā-rā and pa-rā-mo-dā and note that the long vowel arrives one syllable earlier in the second. Under speed, reciters produce one of these twice and drop the other, and because the names are adjacent the ear does not catch it.

Manomayī is manas plus mayī, with the final s of manas becoming o before a voiced sound; the same change produces manoratha, manohara and a hundred other familiar compounds. Knowing it means you will never be tempted to look for a word mano.

In archanā the datives are viśvamātre — an ṛ-stem, so not -yai but -re, and the commonest error in the verse — then jagaddhātryai, viśālākṣyai, virāgiṇyai, pragalbhāyai, paramodārāyai, parāmodāyai and manomayyai. The last doubles the y before the ending.

What the verse asks of the reciter is chiefly attention to its swerve. It moves from the largest claim available in the language to a description of a face, then to a denial that she takes colour from anything, then to the vocabulary of poise and generosity, and then to the announcement that the mind doing all this looking is hers. Chanted at speed the sequence passes as a list of compliments. Chanted at the pace the metre actually wants, it is an argument.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya, chapter 5 (the litany of yā devī verses; numbering varies between editions)
crossReferences.deva: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु मातृरूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu mātṛrūpeṇa saṃsthitā | namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: The goddess who abides in all beings in the form of the mother: to her homage, to her homage, to her homage again and again.
crossReferences.relevance: The classic statement of the position compressed into viśvamātā. The litany's grammar is worth noticing: the goddess is not said to be the mother of all beings from outside them but to stand within all beings in the form of motherhood, which is closer to what the sahasranāma means when it puts viśvamātā and manomayī in the same verse.

crossReferences.iast: tasmād vā etasmāt prāṇamayāt | anyo 'ntara ātmā manomayaḥ |
crossReferences.translation: Other than and within this self made of breath is a self made of mind.
crossReferences.relevance: The source of the word manomaya and of the scheme that gives it its sense. The Upaniṣad's point is that mind is a sheath — real, but not the innermost thing — and reading manomayī against it keeps the name from collapsing into the modern notion that the goddess is a mental construct. She is what that layer is made of, on the way further in.

crossReferences.deva: विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः । रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते ॥
crossReferences.iast: viṣayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ | rasavarjaṃ raso 'py asya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate ||
crossReferences.translation: Objects of sense turn away from the embodied one who abstains from them, but the taste for them remains; even that taste turns away when he has seen the highest.
crossReferences.relevance: The distinction the Gītā draws here is the one virāgiṇī depends on. Dispassion produced by abstention still has the colour in it; dispassion that follows on seeing something better does not. This is why the hymn can set a name of uncolouredness immediately beside parāmodā, supreme gladness, without contradiction.

references.title: Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition
references.author: David Kinsley (University of California Press, 1986)
references.note: The standard survey, and the quickest way to find out which of the epithets in a verse like this are also independent goddesses with temples and festivals attached. Kinsley is descriptive rather than theological, which is what you want when checking whether a name is a description or a proper noun.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: Sanskrit and English on facing pages with notes that tell you where the text is uncertain. Read the whole of the Taittirīya's second section rather than the single line quoted above; the sheaths only make sense as a series, and manomayī is the third term of that series.

references.title: An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa
references.author: tr. Daniel H. H. Ingalls (Harvard Oriental Series 44, 1965)
references.note: Not a religious book at all, and the best possible gloss on viśālākṣī and pragalbhā. Ingalls's introductions explain the conventions of describing eyes, and the classification of heroines by maturity, from inside the literary culture that produced them — which is the same culture that produced this hymn's second line.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up rāga and āmoda together. The first shows how a word for dyeing became the word for passion and for a musical mode; the second shows gladness and diffusive fragrance sharing an entry. Both names in this verse are built on the double sense, and no translation preserves it.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House / Adyar)
references.note: Useful in this verse for seeing how a traditional commentator handles names that are merely complimentary in appearance. The commentary's habit is to find a doctrinal reading for every epithet, including the ones that look like ordinary poetic praise, and comparing that habit with the plain sense is a good exercise in judgement.
